ops.old: Studies published in JAMA have shown that MIPS quality scores are more strongly predicted by specialty and measure selection strategy than by independently-assessed clinical quality.
ops.new: Research has found that MIPS scores track poorly with independently measured quality (see the JAMA study discussed below).
ops.claim: "Studies in JAMA" show MIPS scores predicted by specialty and measure selection more than quality
ops.sources: Bond AM, Schpero WL, Casalino LP, Zhang M, Khullar D, JAMA 2022;328(21):2136-46 (80,246 PCPs, 2019; MIPS scores inconsistently associated with process/outcome performance; low-scoring high performers served sicker, lower-income patients)
ops.note: Unidentifiable study claim reduced to what the real JAMA study shows.

ops.old: A 2019 JAMA Internal Medicine study by Liao and colleagues found that MIPS scores were poorly correlated with independently measured quality metrics. High MIPS scores did not predict better performance on the CMS Overall Quality Star Rating or on HEDIS measures. The authors concluded that MIPS was measuring reporting compliance rather than care quality. A subsequent 2022 analysis in Health Affairs confirmed these findings, showing that the correlation between MIPS performance scores and patient outcomes was statistically indistinguishable from zero for most conditions.
ops.new: A 2022 study in JAMA by Bond, Khullar and colleagues examined 80,246 primary care physicians in the 2019 performance year and found that MIPS scores were inconsistently associated with performance on process and outcome measures: some physicians with low MIPS scores performed well on outcomes, and those physicians tended to serve sicker, lower-income patients. The authors concluded that MIPS may be ineffective at measuring and incentivizing quality improvement.
ops.claim: 2019 JAMA Internal Medicine study by Liao et al.: MIPS scores did not predict Star Rating/HEDIS; 2022 Health Affairs: correlation with outcomes indistinguishable from zero
ops.sources: Bond AM, Schpero WL, Casalino LP, Zhang M, Khullar D, JAMA 2022;328(21):2136-46 (80,246 PCPs, 2019; MIPS scores inconsistently associated with process/outcome performance; low-scoring high performers served sicker, lower-income patients)
ops.note: No such Liao 2019 or 2022 Health Affairs studies; replaced with the real JAMA 2022 study.
